egm-pm-001.question: Routine check of a dual-chamber pacemaker (DDD, lower rate 60 bpm, sensed AV delay 160 ms, maximum tracking rate 130 bpm) implanted for paroxysmal AV block. The patient is at rest and asymptomatic. How do you interpret this tracing?
options: Sequential AP-VP pacing at the lower rate, with no intrinsic atrial activity
Atrial tracking: sensed sinus P waves (AS) followed by VP at the end of the AV delay
Intrinsic AV conduction with pseudofusion: the V spikes fall within native QRS complexes
Atrial double counting: each P wave is counted twice on the atrial channel
commentaires: Incorrect: there is no atrial spike, and the rate (72 bpm) is above the lower rate (60 bpm).
Correct: each AS (with no spike on the A EGM) is followed by a VP 160 ms later, at 833 ms, i.e. 72 bpm.
Incorrect: the RV EGM shows a broad evoked response after each spike, not a pre-existing native QRS.
Incorrect: there is a single atrial marker per cycle, at a regular interval of 833 ms.
egm-pm-001.explication: Read the marker channel first: atrial events above the line (AS = sensed P wave, AP = paced P wave), ventricular events below (VS/VP), with the A-A and V-V intervals in ms. Here, each AS at 833 ms (72 bpm) triggers a VP after the programmed AV delay of 160 ms: this is normal atrial tracking in DDD mode ("VDD" behaviour). The atrial EGM shows no spike, confirming that the P waves are intrinsic; a rate above the lower rate rules out sequential AP-VP pacing. The ventricular evoked response visible on the RV EGM and on the far-field EGM confirms capture. Good habit: read the markers, then check on the EGMs that every marker corresponds to a real signal.
egm-pm-001.aRetenir: AS followed by VP at a fixed delay = normal atrial tracking in DDD: read the markers, then match them against the EGMs.

egm-pm-002.question: A 72-year-old woman had a DDD pacemaker implanted 3 years ago for sinus node dysfunction; before implantation her intrinsic PR interval was 170 ms with narrow QRS complexes. The sensed AV delay has been left at 160 ms and the ventricular pacing reduction algorithm is switched off. At follow-up: 95% ventricular pacing. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Change nothing: atrial tracking with VP is the expected behaviour of DDD mode
Offer an upgrade to CRT straight away to prevent pacing-induced cardiomyopathy
Shorten the AV delay to 120 ms to guarantee complete and stable ventricular capture
Check intrinsic AV conduction, then enable an RV pacing reduction algorithm
commentaires: Incorrect: the device is technically working normally, but the programming is inappropriate for the indication.
Incorrect: an upgrade is considered in heart failure with reduced LVEF and a high RV pacing burden, not as prevention here.
Incorrect: shortening the AV delay would further increase RV pacing, which is harmful in the long term.
Correct: an AV delay of 160 ms, shorter than the 170 ms PR interval, forces unnecessary RV pacing in a patient with no conduction disease.
egm-pm-002.explication: In sinus node dysfunction with preserved AV conduction, RV pacing is unnecessary and, at a high burden, associated with heart failure and AF; the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend minimising it through programming. Here, the 160 ms AV delay, shorter than the intrinsic PR interval, "steals" conduction: every AS is followed by a VP. Intrinsic conduction should be checked (temporary AV delay extension), then AV hysteresis/AV search or a conduction-preserving mode enabled, depending on the manufacturer. Beware of a very long PR interval (> 300 ms), where an excessive AV delay may be poorly tolerated. Good habit: when the VP percentage is high, ask whether the patient really needs it.
egm-pm-002.aRetenir: A high RV pacing percentage in a patient with preserved conduction is a programming error that must be corrected.

egm-pm-003.question: DDD pacemaker implanted for syncope; sensed AV delay programmed at 150 ms with dynamic shortening on exertion. Tracing recorded while walking in the corridor. Statement: this tracing proves that the patient has permanent AV conduction disease.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: a VP delivered 120 ms after each P wave may simply pre-empt normal AV conduction.
Correct: consistent ventricular pacing proves nothing about intrinsic conduction, which is masked by the programmed AV delay.
egm-pm-003.explication: The tracing shows atrial tracking at 667 ms (90 bpm) with an AS-VP interval of 120 ms, shortened by the rate-adaptive AV delay algorithm. A VP delivered 120 ms after the P wave pre-empts any intrinsic conduction if the patient's PR interval is longer: consistent pacing masks AV conduction rather than demonstrating its absence. To find out whether the patient conducts, the AV delay must be temporarily extended (or a conduction test used) while watching for VS events. This confusion leads to patients being wrongly labelled as having "AV block" and to high VP percentages being left unchallenged. Good habit: a VP is never proof of block.
egm-pm-003.aRetenir: Consistent VP masks AV conduction: only extending the AV delay can test it.

egm-pm-004.question: DDD pacemaker implanted 2 years ago for paroxysmal second-degree Mobitz II AV block, lower rate 60 bpm; sensed AV delay extended to 250 ms (AV hysteresis). The remote monitoring nurse is worried because there are no spikes on this EGM. Statement: the absence of pacing indicates pacemaker failure.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: the absence of spikes here reflects appropriate inhibition by intrinsic activity.
Correct: each sensed P wave is conducted (VS 190 ms later, before the 250 ms AV delay times out); the pacemaker is being inhibited normally.
egm-pm-004.explication: The tracing shows AS then VS at 190 ms, at 882 ms (68 bpm): intrinsic AV conduction occurs before the programmed AV delay (250 ms) expires, inhibiting ventricular pacing; a sinus rate above the lower rate also inhibits atrial pacing. This is exactly what we want in a patient with paroxysmal AV block: pacing only when needed. Device failure would show as pauses without spikes while the rate falls below the lower rate, or as spikes without capture. Good habit: a "silent" pacemaker with an intrinsic rhythm above the lower rate is a pacemaker that is working.
egm-pm-004.aRetenir: No spikes + intrinsic rhythm above the lower rate = normal inhibition, not a malfunction.

egm-pm-005.question: Follow-up of a DDD pacemaker implanted for paroxysmal AV block. You review this tracing at the start of the clinic visit. What can you conclude about ventricular pacing?
options: Nothing about capture: no VP is delivered, so only a threshold test can assess it
Ventricular capture is effective, since every P wave is followed by a QRS
The capture threshold must be low, since the lead is sensing correctly
The ventricular lead has probably dislodged, since no VP is seen
commentaires: Correct: a conducted rhythm tells you about sensing (VS, large R wave), not about capture.
Incorrect: these QRS complexes are intrinsic (VS); they say nothing about whether a VP would capture.
Incorrect: good sensing does not rule out a high pacing threshold.
Incorrect: the absence of VP is normal here (inhibition by intrinsic conduction).
egm-pm-005.explication: On this tracing, all ventricular activations are intrinsic (VS 190 ms after each AS): sensing can be assessed (clear R wave on the RV EGM, correct marker annotation), but pacing cannot. Yet it is capture that will protect the patient on the day AV block recurs. Sensing and pacing threshold are two distinct properties of the lead-myocardium interface: a large R wave can coexist with a high threshold (fibrosis, microdislodgement). Good habit: never conclude that "all is well" from a tracing without pacing; measure the threshold (or check the automatic capture algorithm).
egm-pm-005.aRetenir: An intrinsic rhythm tests sensing, not capture: the threshold must be measured.

egm-pm-006.question: An 81-year-old man with a DDD pacemaker for sinus node dysfunction and first-degree AV block, rate response off, lower rate 60 bpm. He complains of breathlessness and fatigue as soon as he climbs one flight of stairs. Histogram: 85% of cycles between 60 and 70 bpm, 90% atrial pacing. This tracing was recorded while walking in the corridor. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Permanently increase the lower rate to 80 bpm
Enable mode switching to avoid tracking atrial arrhythmias
Enable rate response (DDDR) and reassess the exercise response
Shorten the AV delay to improve ventricular filling
commentaires: Incorrect: a higher fixed rate paces unnecessarily at rest without adapting to exercise.
Incorrect: the tracing shows no atrial arrhythmia; the problem is the lack of rate acceleration.
Correct: AP-VP at 1000 ms while walking and a "flat" histogram indicate chronotropic incompetence, an indication for rate response.
Incorrect: the AV delay is not the problem; the rate remains stuck at 60 bpm.
egm-pm-006.explication: The tracing shows sequential AP-VP pacing at 1000 ms (60 bpm), the lower rate, while the patient is walking: the sinus node does not accelerate and, without a sensor, nothing replaces that acceleration. A histogram concentrated between 60 and 70 bpm confirms chronotropic incompetence. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend rate-adaptive pacing in patients with symptomatic chronotropic incompetence; the slope should then be adjusted and the response checked (walk test, histogram). Increasing the lower rate does not help on exertion and adds pacing at rest. Good habit: always cross-check exertional symptoms against the rate histogram.
egm-pm-006.aRetenir: Flat histogram + exertional symptoms = chronotropic incompetence: think rate response.

egm-pm-007.question: Follow-up of a DDD pacemaker (lower rate 60 bpm, paced AV delay 180 ms). What can be stated from this tracing? (select all that apply)
options: Pacing is occurring at the lower rate (AP-AP interval of 1000 ms)
Each VP is followed by a ventricular evoked response: V capture is effective
The patient has no intrinsic AV conduction, otherwise VS events would appear
Pacing is asynchronous, as with a magnet, since no event is sensed
Atrial fibrillation is being masked by continuous atrial pacing
commentaires: Correct: AP-AP and VP-VP at 1000 ms, i.e. 60 bpm.
Correct: the RV EGM and the far-field EGM show a broad evoked complex after each spike.
Incorrect: an AV delay of 180 ms may pre-empt intrinsic AV conduction that is simply slower than 180 ms.
Incorrect: nothing proves asynchronous pacing; with no intrinsic activity, an inhibited mode also paces at the lower rate.
Incorrect: the atrium is captured by every AP, with no fibrillatory activity on the A EGM.
egm-pm-007.explication: The tracing shows AP followed by VP 180 ms later, at 1000 ms: sequential pacing at the lower rate, with visible ventricular capture (evoked response on the RV EGM and on the far-field EGM). The absence of AV conduction cannot be inferred: the programmed AV delay may simply be shorter than the intrinsic conduction time. Nor can asynchronous pacing be asserted: in the absence of intrinsic events, an inhibited DDD mode produces exactly this tracing; only an intrinsic event occurring during the recording would settle the question. Good habit: distinguish what the tracing shows from what it cannot show.
egm-pm-007.aRetenir: AP-VP at the lower rate proves capture, not the absence of conduction or asynchronous pacing.

egm-pm-008.question: A 79-year-old man with complete AV block and a dual-chamber pacemaker programmed DDI 60 bpm because of frequent paroxysmal AF; the RV lead was implanted 3 weeks ago. He phones about brief dizzy spells. What is your diagnosis on this interrogation tracing?
options: Ventricular oversensing inhibiting pacing during the pauses
Ventricular undersensing with spikes falling in the refractory period
Intermittent ventricular loss of capture, non-conducted P waves: pauses
Pseudofusion: V spikes superimposed on simultaneous native QRS complexes
commentaires: Incorrect: with oversensing there would be no spike (inhibition); here VP events are delivered at 1000 ms.
Incorrect: undersensing implies unsensed intrinsic ventricular activity; there is none.
Correct: three V spikes are followed by no evoked response, while the P waves (AS) continue without being conducted.
Incorrect: there are no native QRS complexes, only isolated spikes with no response.
egm-pm-008.explication: VP events are delivered regularly at 1000 ms (60 bpm, DDI mode: AS events at 750 ms are not tracked), but three of them are followed by no evoked complex on either the RV EGM or the far-field EGM: this is loss of capture. As the patient is in complete AV block, the P waves are not conducted and each failure produces ventricular asystole of 2 s or more. Three weeks after implantation, lead dislodgement (or microdislodgement) or a threshold rise related to lead maturation should be considered. Good habit: spike without response = capture problem; no spike = sensing problem.
egm-pm-008.aRetenir: Spike without an evoked response = loss of capture; pause without a spike = oversensing.

egm-pm-009.question: An 84-year-old woman in complete AV block with a dual-chamber pacemaker programmed DDI 60 bpm is referred for presyncope. This tracing is obtained at interrogation. What is the first action to take?
options: Immediately increase V amplitude and pulse width, then measure the threshold
First measure the R wave by lowering the lower rate to 30 bpm
Reduce ventricular sensitivity to prevent inappropriate inhibition
Arrange a follow-up in one month with a chest X-ray
commentaires: Correct: the priority is to restore reliable capture in a pacing-dependent patient, before looking for the cause.
Incorrect: lowering the rate in a patient with no escape rhythm exposes her to prolonged asystole.
Incorrect: the problem is capture, not sensing; sensitivity makes no difference.
Incorrect: delaying exposes her to syncope or death; the problem must be corrected immediately.
egm-pm-009.explication: The tracing shows VP events without an evoked response in a patient whose P waves are not conducted: every loss of capture is a pause. The first step is to make the patient safe: programme a high ventricular output (amplitude and pulse width) and confirm capture on the EGM and ECG. Next come the threshold, impedance (conductor fracture, connection problem), chest X-ray (dislodgement), a search for a metabolic or drug cause (hyperkalaemia, class I antiarrhythmic drug) and the decision on lead revision. Good habit: in a pacing-dependent patient, make safe first, understand later.
egm-pm-009.aRetenir: Loss of capture in a pacing-dependent patient: increase the output immediately, then investigate.

egm-pm-010.question: A 79-year-old man in complete AV block, RV lead implanted 3 weeks ago; loss of capture on this tracing, V output already made safe. Ventricular threshold measured at 2.0 V at 0.4 ms (0.6 V at 0.4 ms at implantation), impedance stable at 610 Ω, no automatic capture algorithm. Which measures are appropriate? (select all that apply)
options: Programme at least 4.0 V at 0.4 ms (2:1 amplitude safety margin)
Programme 2.5 V at 0.4 ms: a 0.5 V margin is enough if impedance is stable
Look for lead dislodgement with a comparative chest X-ray
Conclude that there is a conductor fracture given the threshold rise
commentaires: Correct: the standard margin is twice the threshold in amplitude (or three times in pulse width).
Incorrect: a 0.5 V margin is insufficient given threshold fluctuations, especially early on.
Correct: a threshold rise at 3 weeks means dislodgement or microdislodgement must be excluded.
Incorrect: a fracture raises impedance; here it is stable.
egm-pm-010.explication: Beyond the early post-implant period, the usual safety margin is twice the threshold in amplitude (at the same pulse width) or three times in pulse width; a margin of a few tenths of a volt exposes the patient to further loss of capture when the threshold fluctuates (sleep, drugs, hyperkalaemia). A threshold that has tripled at 3 weeks with stable impedance suggests microdislodgement or an inflammatory reaction at the interface: comparative chest X-ray and close threshold follow-up, with lead revision if the threshold keeps rising. A fracture is associated with high or unstable impedance. Good habit: a 2:1 amplitude margin and a systematic search for the cause.
egm-pm-010.aRetenir: Capture safety margin: 2 × the threshold in amplitude; an early rising threshold means looking for dislodgement.

egm-pm-011.question: A 68-year-old woman with a DDD pacemaker (lower rate 60 bpm) implanted for complete AV block, atrial sensitivity programmed at 1.0 mV. Routine follow-up. What is the main problem visible on this tracing?
options: Atrial loss of capture due to a rise in pacing threshold
Far-field R-wave oversensing causing AR events
Normal function: atrial rate hysteresis is active
Atrial undersensing: intrinsic P waves are not marked
commentaires: Incorrect: the AP events without an atrial response fall shortly after an unsensed P wave, while the atrium is still refractory; the other AP events capture, so the threshold is not the issue.
Incorrect: there are no AR markers on this tracing.
Incorrect: hysteresis explains neither visible P waves without markers nor AP events delivered just after an intrinsic P wave.
Correct: most of the low-amplitude P waves have no marker; the pacemaker therefore delivers AP events at 1000 ms, competing with sinus rhythm.
egm-pm-011.explication: On the atrial EGM, sinus rhythm (about 78 bpm) is faster than the lower rate, but only a few of the larger P waves are marked AS; the others, of low amplitude, have no marker. The pacemaker, which "does not see" them, carries on pacing the atrium at the lower rate (AP 1000 ms after the last sensed or paced atrial event): the AP events fall shortly after an unsensed P wave. Some produce no atrial response because the atrium has just depolarised and is still refractory (functional non-capture, unrelated to the threshold); others, falling later, do capture: this is competitive atrial pacing due to undersensing. Each atrial event is followed by a VP at 170-180 ms, as expected in this patient with complete AV block. Causes to look for: a sensitivity value set too high relative to P-wave amplitude, variable P waves (posture, respiration), atrial lead maturation or dislodgement. Good habit: every atrial deflection on the EGM should have its marker; a deflection without a marker (outside blanking) = undersensing.
egm-pm-011.aRetenir: A P wave visible on the EGM without a marker = atrial undersensing, a cause of competitive atrial pacing.

egm-pm-012.question: A patient in complete AV block with a DDD pacemaker shows the atrial undersensing seen on this tracing: measured P-wave amplitude varies from 0.6 to 1.5 mV from beat to beat, with bipolar atrial sensitivity programmed at 1.0 mV. Which change corrects the problem?
options: Programme 2.0 mV to make the atrial channel more selective and more reliable
Programme 0.3 mV, then check that far-field signals are not being sensed
Increase atrial amplitude to make capture of the AP events more secure
Extend the PVARP to eliminate competitive atrial pacing
commentaires: Incorrect: increasing the value in mV makes the channel less sensitive and worsens undersensing.
Correct: "increasing sensitivity" = lowering the value in mV; 0.3 mV gives a 2:1 margin on the smallest P wave.
Incorrect: the AP events without a response fall in the refractory period, so this is not a threshold problem; more energy would not remove the competition.
Incorrect: the PVARP does not affect sensing of P waves occurring outside the refractory period.
egm-pm-012.explication: The sensitivity value is a threshold: the lower it is in mV, the more sensitive the channel. With P waves of 0.6 to 1.5 mV, a 1.0 mV threshold misses the smallest ones. The practical rule is to programme a value no more than half (ideally a third) of the smallest measured amplitude: here 0.3 mV. The chosen value must remain programmable in bipolar sensing; if undersensing persists despite this, a lead problem should be suspected. After the change, check that the far-field R wave is not being sensed (AR markers at a fixed interval just after the QRS) and that there are no spurious mode-switch episodes. Good habit: always say "value in mV" to avoid getting the direction wrong.
egm-pm-012.aRetenir: To correct undersensing, lower the sensitivity value (in mV), with a 2:1 to 3:1 margin.
